newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Israel's Sharansky returns to Ukraine, seeks trade.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Sharansky returns to Ukraine, seeks trade.

text.p: Natan Sharansky, Soviet dissident turned Israeli minister, on Wednesday paid homage to Jews massacred by Nazis outside the Ukrainian capital in a pilgrimage he was banned from making in Soviet days.

Sharansky, 49, who formed a political party in Israel after he left the Soviet Union in a dramatic Cold War spy swap, returned to the country of his birth to promote trade in his role as minister of commerce and trade.

"I feel a great weight and at the same time, I feel how important it is that people remember," Sharansky told reporters as he reflected on his first visit to two monuments near Kiev to the dead of Babi Yar, one of the Nazi's first killing fields.
Sharansky was born in the Ukrainian city of Donetsk but he left in the late 1960s for Russia, where he was thrown into a Soviet prison charged with spying in 1978.
His release nine years into a 13-year sentence was assisted by an international campaign to support the defender of Jewish rights in the former Soviet Union.
On Wednesday he visited Babi Yar, where more than 100,000 people, mostly Jews, were shot in the 1940s. The site was marked by a Jewish menorah after the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
"This is my first visit because when I tried before I wasn't permitted. Before there was no place, no memorial, nothing. They always wanted us not to know a thing," Sharansky said.
"But then it was Israel that reminded us we are Jews. And we decided to try and find out what it means. And then we found out we were living in the killing fields of the holocaust," he said.
Surrounded by members of Ukraine's 500,000-strong Jewish community, he stood at the edge of the ravine where bodies were dumped after being shot in the neck by SS guards.
"Just imagine, Sharansky standing here and talking about the killings. Of course I had to come and see that. It could never have happened a few years ago," said Raisa Prosyanikova, 61.
Sharansky also laid a wreath at a modern grey sculpture Soviet authorities erected some distance from the actual ravine.

"When this monument was erected with no signs of Jewishness, Jewish activists from many cities who tried to come here for a special ceremony were taken from the trains and put under house arrest," he told reporters.

Independent Ukraine's leaders have worked hard to eradicate longstanding mistrust between Ukrainians and Jews fuelled by Tsarist pogroms, collaboration with Nazi occupiers and discrimination in the Soviet era.
Sharansky's trip marked a new stage in relations between the two states, sealed in 1995 during a visit by Yitzhak Rabin.

Opening a trade exhibition on Monday called "Israel only", Sharansky welcomed increased trade -- put at $62.27 million in exports from Israel and $47.23 million in goods from Ukraine last year -- but said much more had to be done.
"We have a history which ties us together closely, for good or bad...We have a common culture," Sharansky said, referring to a Ukrainian-Jewish community of about 300,000 people in Israel.
Sharansky and Ukrainian Foreign Trade Minister Serhiy Osyka signed a memorandum on liberalising trade on Tuesday and the Israeli minister said trade could grow to $1 billion by 2000.
